title: Weekly Top Five Articles: What Fills the Soul When Formation Fails
author: Anthony B. Bradley
source: Anthony B. Bradley (Substack) -- Weekly Top Five roundup
summary: Anthony B. Bradley's weekly curated digest of five articles is themed around what happens when interior formation fails and something else -- a wound, a tribe, a machine, social media -- moves in to organize the soul instead. Article 1 (Scott Barry Kaufman, Skeptic): anti-woke intellectuals split into two types -- those who criticize bad ideas revisably and those consumed by unhealed grievance -- demonstrating that victimhood as identity belongs to no single political alignment. Article 2 (Jesse Smith and Jane Lankes Smith, IFStudies): families, far more than church programs, determine whether faith survives into adulthood; faith travels through embodied love at the table and in ordinary conflict repair. Article 3 (Geoff Shullenberger, Hedgehog Review): half a century of academic antihumanism has been automated by generative AI, leaving the humanities with no doctrine of the human person left to defend. Article 4 (Vladimir Hedrih, PsyPost): people who pray for their romantic partners report higher relationship satisfaction, the effect concentrating among the genuinely devout. Article 5 (Karina Petrova, PsyPost): racial resentment increases voter turnout among white, Asian, and Latino evangelicals while suppressing it among Black evangelicals -- showing how religious identity can function as a vehicle for tribal grievance rather than a check on it.
points: A wound left unmetabolized becomes a liturgy (Kaufman): aggrieved victimhood runs identically across political alignments; the diagnostic question for any crusade is whether it is driven by genuine reform impulse or by an injury that cannot be named.

Faith travels through embodied love, not programs (Smith/Lankes Smith): American religious decline is a household formation crisis -- parental modeling, marital quality, and warm parent-child relationships do the heaviest lifting; church programs scaffold what households build but cannot pour the foundation.

The humanities have no doctrine of the human left to defend against AI (Shullenberger): decades of academic antihumanism produced a culture unable to articulate what is worth protecting when trillion-dollar enterprises come to automate what remains.

Petitionary prayer is daily rehearsal in willing another person's good (Hedrih/Fincham): orienting attention toward the beloved's flourishing does real measurable relational work, concentrated among the genuinely devout.

When formation is thin, faith becomes a flag for the tribe (Petrova/Chan): the asymmetry between white and Black evangelical political mobilization around racial resentment reveals a formation failure -- discipleship should be a school for the soul, not a vehicle for grievance.
quotes: What holds a person is an interior life built slowly through love, practice, and communion. When interior architecture of a person is never built, or is allowed to collapse, something else moves in to organize the soul, usually a wound, a tribe, a machine, social media.
Kaufman calls the crusade a bandage that never comes off because the cut is never allowed to heal. The diagnostic question: am I doing this to repair the world or to repair an injury?

Smith and Lankes Smith marshal data on American adults raised Christian to show that families, far more than programs or pastors, determine whether faith survives into adulthood, with parental modeling, marital quality, and warm parent-child relationships doing the heaviest lifting.

A congregation can scaffold what a household builds, but it cannot pour the foundation. The report's quiet emphasis on fathers and on stable marriages names what the contemplative tradition always assumed, that belief is caught inside relationships before it is taught.

Shullenberger argues that a half century of academic antihumanism has been overtaken and effectively automated by generative artificial intelligence, leaving the humanities with no doctrine of the human person left to defend.

Where formation is thin, faith becomes a flag for the tribe rather than a school for the soul: identity does the political work that discipleship was meant to do. The asymmetry between the groups is the tell.
